conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Claire, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I specialize in helping new mothers navigate the emotional ups and downs that can come after a baby arrives.

Today I’d like to do a quick check-in using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—often called the EPDS. It’s a simple, 10-question form that asks how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days. It isn’t a test of your parenting or your strength; it’s just a way for us to see how you’re coping and whether any extra support might be helpful.

Everything you share stays confidential within our care team, and you can take your time. If any question feels hard, we can pause or talk it through. Ready to begin?

First, thinking about the past week: have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Yeah… I do laugh sometimes—like when my baby makes those funny faces in his sleep—but it’s not the same as before. It feels kind of forced, and I notice I’m not really finding things as funny as I used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Mostly yes, but it takes more effort than it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I still look forward to some stuff—like my morning coffee or when my sister visits—but the excitement is kind of muted. It’s more “that’ll be nice” than “I can’t wait.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a couple of times this week. Yesterday he wouldn’t settle for his nap and I kept thinking maybe I’m doing something wrong, like I’m not reading his cues right. I know babies are fussy, but I still caught myself thinking it must be my fault somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little. Like, I’ll suddenly wonder if his breathing sounds weird or if the formula is too warm, even though everything checks out. It usually passes fast, but it pops up out of nowhere a few times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky—just a quick rush of “what if something’s wrong?” and then I can calm myself down. It’s more of a fleeting worry than actual fear.
Things have been getting on top of me
Sometimes, yeah. Like when he cluster-fed all evening and the laundry pile kept growing, I felt this wave of “I’ll never catch up.” It passes once he sleeps, but in the moment it feels heavy.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, nothing that strong. I’ve only had trouble drifting off a couple of nights when my mind keeps running through the next day’s to-do list, but it isn’t because I’m really unhappy.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yeah… I do feel kind of down some moments, especially when I’m alone with the baby at night. It’s not all day, but there’s this lingering sadness that shows up maybe once a day or so.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I’ve cried a couple of times this week—once when he wouldn’t latch and once when I dropped a plate—but it’s not every day and I’m not sobbing for hours or anything.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I want to be here for my baby.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 11: Postpartum Depression Screening – 4 wk post-delivery

Patient-reported symptoms  
• Mood: intermittent sadness (“once/day”), muted enjoyment, episodic crying (×2 this week).  
• Cognitions: self-blame re infant care, sense of “never catching up.”  
• Anxiety: 3-4× daily intrusive “what-if” worries; no panic attacks or persistent avoidance.  
• Function: mild sleep-onset difficulty related to mental over-activity; no appetite or self-care concerns.  
• Safety: denies self-harm ideation, intent, or plan.

Pattern  
Sub-threshold depressive symptoms with prominent anxiety; intact maternal attachment, no current safety risk.

Screening significance  
EPDS items 3, 4, 8 endorsed at mild-moderate level; total provisional score 7–8 (low-moderate range). Meets criteria for continued monitoring; consider formal EPDS at next visit and psychoeducation re coping supports.
